strengths: Novel and compelling task formulation: Reconstructing and animating high-fidelity 3D head avatars across an individual's lifelong spectrum from unstructured, in-the-wild collections moves beyond conventional momentary/short-clip avatar reconstruction.

Well-motivated technical design: Formulating the personalized space as an additive neural linear combination of a shared canonical representation and adaptive neural head bases (via Dynamo) provides an elegant balance between shared identity priors and moment-specific variations.

Effective 2DGS integration and meshing: Extending 2D Gaussian surfels with FLAME-guided deformation (DNA-2DGS) and introducing Defer-Warping enables plausible dynamic surface meshing without suffering from per-frame Poisson reconstruction overhead.

Comprehensive dataset and thorough evaluation: The curation of TimeWalker-1.0 (40 celebrities, >2.7M frames across decades) provides a valuable benchmark. The paper presents rigorous quantitative and qualitative comparisons across multiple protocols against diverse baselines (NeRF, 3DGS, generative, and one-shot methods), along with insightful downstream application experiments.
weaknesses: Reliance on monocular tracking and FLAME priors: The framework relies heavily on FLAME mesh tracking and camera parameter estimation from in-the-wild images. As acknowledged by the authors, tracking errors, inaccurate expressions, and complex occlusions (e.g., extreme hairstyles, accessories) in historical footage directly degrade Gaussian surfel deformation and geometry.

Residual lighting and appearance entanglement: As shown in the supplementary analysis (Sec. F.4 and Fig. 13), separating ambient illumination from intrinsic lifestage appearance remains incomplete when solely using residual latent embeddings.

Limited view extrapolation: Performance degrades noticeably at large yaw angles (>45 degrees, Fig. 12) due to sparse profile views in unstructured collections, highlighting an inherent challenge of unconstrained monocular inputs.

Minor editorial inconsistencies: Minor cross-referencing mismatches exist in the text (e.g., on page 8, the Dynamo ablation refers to Tab. 8 instead of Tab. 3 in the main paper; minor typo 'TimeWawlker-1.0' in Table 7 header).

strengths: Novel and compelling problem setup: Extends 3D head avatar creation beyond momentary/short video setups to lifelong modeling across years and decades from unstructured in-the-wild image collections.

Well-motivated technical framework: The additive formulation—combining an invariant canonical average representation, a Dynamic Neural Basis-Blending Module (Dynamo) for compact moment-specific variations, and DNA-2DGS for expression deformation—effectively balances cross-stage shared identity with stage-specific traits.

Strong geometric and rendering quality: Extending 2D Gaussian Surfels with Defer-Warping enables explicit, animatable mesh extraction alongside high-fidelity rendering, mitigating artifacts typical in monocular unstructured captures.

Valuable benchmark and thorough evaluation: The TimeWalker-1.0 dataset (40 celebrities, 2.7M frames) provides a solid testbed. Experiments across two protocols (1-vs-1 and 1-vs-N) against a wide variety of baselines (NeRF-based, 3DGS-based, generative, and one-shot) convincingly demonstrate superior identity preservation and reconstruction quality.
weaknesses: Incomplete disentanglement of lighting and lifestage: As admitted in the supplementary material (Sec. F.4), residual embeddings sometimes entangle lighting variations with lifestage attributes, leading to occasional identity or age drift when interpolating lighting conditions.

Heuristic discretization of lifestages: The framework models life stages primarily as discrete appearance/time clusters with learned blending weights, rather than learning a truly continuous, monotonically constrained chronological aging trajectory.

Strong dependence on FLAME tracking accuracy: Preprocessing relies heavily on FLAME fitting, which can be noisy and error-prone on historic, low-resolution, or non-frontal in-the-wild images, directly impacting deformation gradient computation and oral/expression accuracy.

Minor presentation and citation inconsistencies: Several typographical errors are present (e.g., 'propse' in Section 5, 'scroe' in Table 16, 'TimeWawlker-1.0' in Table 7), and Section 4.5 incorrectly references Table 8 instead of Table 3 from the main text.

strengths: Novel and meaningful task formulation: The paper addresses lifelong head avatar reconstruction from unconstrained, unstructured in-the-wild collections across decades, departing from the prevailing paradigm of momentary or single-video capture.

Well-motivated method: Adapting the classic 3DMM linear combination concept into a neural parametric formulation (combining a canonical average representation with a dynamic basis-blending module, Dynamo) provides an elegant balance between shared identity preservation and moment-specific adaptation.

Effective integration of 2D Gaussian Surfels (DNA-2DGS): Extending 2DGS to dynamic head animation with a Defer-Warping strategy enables both high-fidelity rendering and topologically coherent, dynamic surface mesh extraction.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors conduct extensive comparisons against NeRF-based (INSTA, INSTA++), 3DGS-based (FlashAvatar, Gaussian Surfels), generative (GANAvatar), and one-shot methods (GAGAvatar, GPHM) across two distinct protocols (1 vs 1 and 1 vs N).
Valuable benchmark resource: TimeWalker-1.0, comprising 40 identities spanning 20–80 years of age and 2.7M frames, serves as an impactful contribution for research in long-horizon facial modeling.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on preprocessing and FLAME tracking: In-the-wild collections inherently feature challenging illumination, extreme poses, and non-rigid hair/neck motion. Inaccurate FLAME tracking or face parsing masks can propagate directly into canonical surfel initialization and inverse warping.

Imperfect disentanglement of lighting and aging: As shown in Fig. 13 and discussed in Sec. F.4, residual embeddings partially conflate environmental lighting/color tone with intrinsic aging attributes.

Limited evaluation on identity consistency and perceptual aging: ArcFace identity consistency is only evaluated quantitatively on three identities against GAGAvatar (Tab. 16). Additional evaluation across more identities and a perceptual user study assessing perceived age accuracy vs. identity retention would strengthen the claims.

Degradation under extreme viewpoints: The model exhibits visible artifacts at yaw angles beyond 45 degrees due to sparse coverage in wild data (Fig. 12), pointing to a continuing challenge in geometry hallucination under monocular long-tail capture.
